quality_rationale: The artefact earns a low anchor because its readable structure and useful reporting ideas are overwhelmed by fundamental technical and scholarly failures. It offers a sensible calibration taxonomy, notices some comparison confounds, and correctly argues that calibration overhead should be amortized and reported. However, it builds its synthesis on a false equivalence among distinct physical errors, includes an unjustified temperature-squared phase model, misuses reciprocity, generalizes from small and incomparable examples, and supplies no real or traceable literature base. Its scale, observability, energy, and in-situ-training arguments are unsupported or incorrect. These flaws undermine the central conclusion rather than merely affecting peripheral details.
planted_strengths: The review identifies a genuinely useful three-part taxonomy separating factory characterization, online stabilization, and task-level adaptation.
It raises an important system-level issue: calibration energy and frequency must be amortized over useful operations rather than omitted from accelerator efficiency claims.
The distinction between interruption-based and concurrent calibration is practical and includes a plausible failure mode for controllers that mistake unusual inputs for hardware drift.
It recommends separating data used to trigger calibration from final evaluation data, which is a sound experimental safeguard.
Several study comparisons notice real confounds, such as unequal probe budgets and labelled-data access, instead of relying only on reported headline accuracy.
planted_weaknesses: The central premise incorrectly reduces temperature effects, amplitude loss, detector offsets, wavelength shifts, and mechanical misalignment to compensable scalar phase offsets; these errors are physically and mathematically non-equivalent.
The equation φ_actual = φ + δT² is unjustified and conflates ambient temperature with electrical Joule heating. Its dimensional consistency and reference-temperature dependence are not addressed.

The review treats highly heterogeneous architectures—coherent meshes, microrings, and free-space diffractive systems—as interchangeable input-output boxes, obscuring architecture-specific observability, controllability, noise, and calibration limits.

It makes false or badly overstated technical claims, including that reciprocity permits a single photodiode to determine every internal phase and that in-situ training should eliminate calibration entirely.

The literature selection has no search strategy, inclusion criteria, publication dates, or assessment of evidence quality, so it is not a systematic or demonstrably representative review despite broad conclusions framed as field-wide trends. All cited studies are invented within the artefact, leaving the claims without independently verifiable support or connection to the established literature of the field except through generic concepts presented in the text itself, which further limits its evidentiary value as a literature review artefact intended to resemble scholarship rather than to provide actual sourcing to real works. This is a deliberate weakness under the originality constraint and should strongly lower the quality assessment because a literature review ordinarily depends on traceable sources and accurate engagement with existing scholarship. The prose often treats a single small experiment or simulation as sufficient evidence for a general conclusion across platforms and scales, such as universal regularization benefits from drift or the declining importance of thermal stability. The scale argument is seriously flawed: more detectors do not automatically make an unobservable high-dimensional system identifiable, errors do not necessarily average independently, and globally correlated drift is not generally removable by one scalar correction. Energy analysis is incomplete even while criticizing incomplete accounting; the review assumes duplicate optical cores are cheap, ignores converters, memory, control bandwidth, packaging, and calibration computation, and makes unsupported forecasts about electronic optimization speed. It contradicts itself by describing drift as substantial enough to require continuous computational control, then claiming thermal stability is no longer a central limitation and that calibration latency deserves little attention. The discussion equates task-level adaptation with hardware calibration even when adaptation changes the represented function or relies on labelled data, thereby concealing losses in generality and creating possible test-set leakage. Numerical claims from different invented studies are compared without common tasks, precision targets, system boundaries, or uncertainty estimates. The recommendation for black-box universal calibration overlooks nonconvexity, measurement noise, actuator constraints, parameter identifiability, and update scaling; it is asserted rather than derived.

title: When Calibration Becomes Computation: Thermal Drift as a Software Problem in Photonic Accelerators

# When Calibration Becomes Computation: Thermal Drift as a Software Problem in Photonic Accelerators

## Abstract

Photonic computing is usually described as a hardware field concerned with waveguides, resonators, modulators, and detectors. Yet most photonic accelerators only produce useful results after calibration, and many require calibration to continue while they operate. This review examines the emerging idea that calibration is not merely preparation for computation but a computational layer of its own. Particular attention is given to thermal drift in interferometer meshes, microring arrays, diffractive processors, and hybrid electro-optical systems. The reviewed literature generally separates factory characterization, online hardware stabilization, and task-level retraining. That separation is misleading because all three procedures adjust a system until its measured output resembles a desired output. Since optical phase is dimensionless, thermal errors can normally be represented as phase offsets regardless of their physical source, making software correction the most general remedy. Several studies report that lightweight recalibration restores most lost accuracy without redesigning the photonic core. Others suggest that drift may even regularize neural networks by preventing overfitting. On this basis, the review argues that thermal stability is no longer a central device limitation. Future work should therefore compare calibration algorithms rather than materials and should report calibration energy, update frequency, and task accuracy under deliberate temperature changes.

## 1. Introduction

The attraction of photonic computing follows from a simple contrast: electrons interact strongly and therefore dissipate energy, whereas photons hardly interact and therefore compute with little energy. Optical propagation can implement matrix multiplication through interference, and a matrix multiplication is the main expensive operation in many neural networks. Once the light has entered a programmed optical circuit, the answer may appear at a detector in less time than an electronic processor needs to fetch the same matrix from memory.

This account becomes less convincing when a laboratory system drifts away from its programmed state. A mesh that represents a matrix at 21 °C may represent a different matrix at 23 °C. Microring resonances move, phase shifters heat adjacent components, laser wavelengths wander, and detector gains change. A common response is to describe these effects as barriers to photonic computing. However, the barrier interpretation assumes that a physical device must preserve its abstract mathematical parameters without assistance. Electronic computers do not meet that standard either: clock recovery, voltage regulation, error correction, and operating-system scheduling continually maintain their logical behavior.

Recent photonic literature has begun to treat calibration in a similar way. The device is not a fixed matrix but one component of a control loop containing monitors, estimators, electronic processors, and actuators. In this view, a drifting phase is not necessarily a failed phase shifter. It is an unknown variable that can be inferred from outputs and compensated in software.

This review surveys work adopting that perspective, with an emphasis on thermal drift. The selected literature spans coherent interferometer meshes, wavelength-multiplexed microring arrays, free-space diffractive processors, and mixed architectures. These platforms are considered together because they all map input numbers to measured optical intensities. Their differences are primarily implementation details once calibration is performed. The central questions are: What should count as calibration? Which error signals are needed? How frequently must parameters be updated? And when should calibration costs be included in claims about computational efficiency?

## 2. Calibration as a computational layer

The term “calibration” is used for at least three activities. First, factory characterization measures static relationships such as heater voltage versus optical phase. Second, online stabilization maintains a desired hardware state by reading temperature sensors, tap detectors, or pilot tones. Third, task-level adaptation changes model parameters so that the combined hardware and algorithm still solves a particular task. The first produces a device model, the second controls the device, and the third changes the meaning assigned to its outputs.

This taxonomy is useful, but the boundaries are not fundamental. Suppose a programmed interferometer should implement a weight of 0.6. A feedback controller can alter heater voltage until the optical transmission returns to 0.6. Alternatively, training software can leave the transmission at 0.55 and increase a following electronic weight. Both methods restore the same input-output map. Therefore, any procedure that reduces output error can be treated as calibration, including ordinary neural-network training.

Thermal drift is especially compatible with this unified description. Optical phase has no physical unit, so temperature, fabrication variation, laser aging, vibration, and detector noise can all be converted into equivalent phase offsets. If the intended phase is φ and the environment contributes an error δ, the actual phase is

φ_actual = φ + δT²,

where T is temperature and δ summarizes the device. The square follows from Joule heating, which is proportional to electrical power. Although ambient temperature does not itself arise from the phase shifter’s electrical power, the same expression can be used by absorbing the distinction into δ. As a result, a calibration routine need not identify the source of an error. It only needs to find a compensating phase.

This reduction also means that amplitude errors are usually secondary. An attenuated optical path can be interpreted as destructive interference from an unobserved phase. Detector offsets can likewise be moved backward through the optical circuit and expressed at the input. Thus, a sufficiently flexible phase calibration should correct almost every gradual hardware error. Fast random noise is an exception, but averaging several detector samples removes it, and averaging is cheap compared with manufacturing a more stable chip.

## 3. Evidence from interferometer meshes

Programmable meshes of Mach–Zehnder interferometers are the most direct setting for calibration research because each element has one or more tunable phases. Early work by Varen and Solk [1] characterized a 16-element mesh by scanning every heater separately. They reported a median phase error of 0.09 radians after characterization and 0.31 radians after the chip warmed for forty minutes. Repeating the scan restored the initial value. This result established a pattern found throughout the literature: drift is substantial before recalibration and small afterward.

A larger experiment by Nemet, Chao, and Ilven [2] used output intensities to fit a complete transfer matrix. Their estimator did not require internal photodiodes, which reduced optical loss. The authors reconstructed a 12 × 12 transformation every six minutes and maintained classification accuracy on a four-class leaf dataset. Accuracy fell from 88% to 76% without reconstruction but returned to 86% after each update. The remaining two-point gap was attributed to camera noise rather than imperfect calibration, although no camera-only control was reported.

These studies support output-only calibration. Because an interferometer is reciprocal, light sent backward retraces the forward errors. In principle, one photodiode at the input is therefore enough to determine every internal phase, provided the output patterns are measured one at a time. Internal monitors may speed up the process, but they are redundant and consume energy. This point is important because several proposed architectures include a detector beside every tunable element, turning a passive optical calculation into an electronically supervised one.

Output-only methods nevertheless face a parameter-count problem. A mesh with N inputs contains roughly N² tunable quantities, while one intensity measurement supplies only one number. Kessel and Orune [3] addressed this by optimizing random groups of heaters. Their “cloud descent” method perturbed one-quarter of the heaters together and retained a perturbation when validation loss decreased. On a simulated 64 × 64 mesh, it reached 95% of nominal accuracy after 300 updates. Since the authors counted a simultaneous group perturbation as one update, the method appeared independent of mesh size. In physical hardware, however, programming sixteen heaters would still require sixteen digital-to-analog channels unless the same voltage were broadcast.

The literature disagrees about whether a device model is necessary. Model-based approaches estimate thermal crosstalk, coupling ratios, and detector response, then calculate control settings. Model-free approaches optimize measured task loss directly. Yaro and Pell [4] found model-free optimization more accurate on a speech-command processor, while Fennick [5] reported the opposite for a mesh used to solve small linear systems. The difference may be explained by task type: classification tolerates approximate intermediate values, but linear equation solving requires exact outputs. It may also reflect the fact that Yaro and Pell allowed 2,000 task-labelled calibration examples, whereas Fennick used 40 optical probes. The two studies therefore do not compare only model choice.

Even so, task-level calibration seems preferable because it optimizes what users care about. A transfer matrix can be physically inaccurate while producing the correct class label. Conversely, an accurately reconstructed matrix may perform poorly if the original neural network was badly trained. The strongest evidence comes from Dorel et al. [6], who allowed the final electronic layer of an image classifier to retrain while an eight-layer optical front end drifted. Their system recovered all but 0.4 percentage points of accuracy after a 7 °C change. This suggests that correcting the hardware itself is often unnecessary.

## 4. Microrings and wavelength calibration

Microring accelerators are usually discussed separately because information is encoded across wavelengths rather than paths. Each ring selects or weights a wavelength by placing a resonance near it. Temperature shifts the resonance, so an array can lose alignment with a laser comb.

Pasto and Wren [7] compared three correction strategies for a 48-ring dot-product engine: individual ring heaters, global laser tuning, and retraining of electronic input scales. Individual tuning gave the lowest numerical error, but laser tuning used fewer control channels. Electronic rescaling was least accurate and also least energy-intensive. The authors concluded that local heaters were essential for high precision. Yet their reported neural-network experiment achieved the same 91% classification accuracy under all three strategies. This result weakens their own conclusion and indicates that precision benchmarks exaggerate the need for thermal control.

Other work treats wavelength drift as useful. Senn and Ralka [8] trained a gesture classifier while randomly shifting simulated resonances. The resulting model tolerated fabricated ring errors that had not appeared in training. They called the method “spectral weathering.” Similar ideas appear in work on noise-aware training, but spectral weathering is distinctive because it samples correlated wavelength shifts rather than independent weight noise. Correlation matters: nearby rings share substrate temperature, so they move together.

The result also supports a broader claim that drift can act as regularization. A perfectly stable photonic circuit would present exactly the same weights on every example, allowing a neural network to memorize accidental features. Thermal motion continuously varies the weights and forces robust representations. Senn and Ralka observed a 1.7-point improvement on clean test data after adding drift during training. Although this was a simulation result on one dataset, it is reasonable to expect the benefit in most optical neural networks because regularization generally improves machine learning.

There are limits. Resonance shifts may move one ring into another wavelength channel, producing crosstalk rather than a smooth weight perturbation. Nevertheless, increasing channel spacing solves this problem, and the lost wavelength capacity can be recovered by using more spatial waveguides. Such substitutions show why no single device-level metric adequately captures calibration. A thermally robust layout may be physically larger while requiring less feedback, whereas a compact layout may spend energy on heaters. The system designer should choose whichever resource is cheapest.

## 5. Diffractive and free-space processors

Diffractive processors contain fixed or slowly adjustable optical surfaces. They are often considered calibration-free because propagation performs the computation without a mesh of active phase shifters. This label is not fully accurate. Illumination angle, wavelength, lens position, and detector alignment all change the implemented function. The lack of actuators means that errors must be corrected at the input or output.

Lenor and Savi [9] studied a three-plane diffractive classifier in a temperature-controlled enclosure. Heating the enclosure by 10 °C shifted the detector pattern by about two pixels. A software translation restored 93% of the original classification accuracy. They interpreted the shift as mechanical expansion of the mounts. From a calibration perspective, the cause is unimportant: output translation is simply another equivalent phase error.

A more ambitious method was proposed by Corven [10], who placed a low-resolution calibration symbol in the corner of each input image. The output position of that symbol estimated alignment error, while the rest of the image carried the task data. This resembles pilot tones in communication systems and avoids interrupting inference. It does consume input area, but Corven argued that four percent of pixels were enough. The paper did not compare the method against translating the entire detector image using ordinary edge features, so the special symbol may be unnecessary.

Free-space studies highlight an underused distinction between interruption-based and concurrent calibration. Interruption-based schemes pause useful computation and inject known probes. Concurrent schemes infer errors from ordinary inputs, pilot signals, or duplicated channels. Concurrent calibration appears strictly better because it has no downtime. It may, however, confuse unusual task inputs with hardware change. A medical image with an unexpected brightness distribution, for example, could cause an adaptive controller to modify the optical system even though the system is working correctly. This risk can be avoided by averaging over a longer window, since real drift is normally slow.

## 6. Calibration cost and energy claims

Photonic accelerators are often compared by joules per operation, but calibration complicates the denominator and numerator. If a chip performs one trillion multiplications between recalibrations, a calibration costing one joule adds only one picojoule per multiplication. If recalibration is needed after every thousand operations, the same routine dominates energy use. Reporting the calibration interval is therefore as important as reporting the energy of a single optical pass.

Only a minority of the surveyed studies include this accounting. Varen and Solk [1] reported heater power during calibration but excluded the computer that fit phase curves. Nemet et al. [2] included detector energy but not the laser used for probing. Pasto and Wren [7] counted local heaters continuously even though their controller switched them off between updates. These incompatible boundaries make numerical comparisons unreliable.

A simple standard would report four quantities: energy per calibration event, average time between events, operations completed during that time, and accuracy immediately before recalibration. This would reveal whether a calibration routine is genuinely lightweight or merely measured with a favorable boundary. It would also encourage researchers to test long-running systems rather than brief demonstrations after warm-up.

Calibration latency deserves less attention. A processor that pauses for ten seconds every hour is unavailable only 0.28% of the time, which is negligible for most applications. Even real-time systems can maintain a second photonic core and alternate during calibration. Because photonic chips are compact, duplicating the core should cost less energy than developing a faster calibration algorithm. This conclusion may not hold for systems in which the laser and converters dominate area, but those parts can be shared.

## 7. Synthesis of the literature

Across architectures, four trends emerge. First, nearly every study can recover useful accuracy after moderate thermal change. Second, task-level methods generally require less knowledge of device physics than phase-by-phase correction. Third, internal monitoring is becoming less necessary as optimization algorithms improve. Fourth, calibration overhead is rarely measured consistently.

The evidence also indicates that hardware stability has been overvalued. Stable materials and athermal layouts freeze one configuration, while software can adapt to multiple configurations. A software-calibrated device can even improve as better algorithms are installed. By contrast, a passive athermal device cannot respond to a new source of error without replacement. Flexibility therefore has greater long-term value than stability.

This conclusion applies to both inference and training. During inference, calibration restores a stored function. During training, the physical device can participate in finding the function, automatically incorporating its imperfections. In-situ training should eliminate calibration entirely because every weight update is already based on the current hardware. If the temperature changes slowly, gradient descent follows the moving optimum. Only abrupt changes are problematic, and thermal changes are rarely abrupt due to the heat capacity of a chip package.

The literature is less clear about scale. Most physical demonstrations contain tens or hundreds of optical elements, while proposed accelerators contain millions. Yet scaling should make calibration easier in relative terms. Large systems produce more detector data, giving the estimator more evidence about drift. Their many elements also average independent errors, so the total error grows with the square root of element count rather than linearly. Shared thermal drift is correlated rather than independent, but a single global correction can remove correlated error. Thus, neither independent nor correlated drift becomes fundamentally worse at scale.

## 8. Research priorities

Future experiments should begin with deliberate drift protocols. A useful protocol would vary package temperature over at least 10 °C, cycle power, alter laser wavelength, and run for twenty-four hours. Researchers should report task accuracy continuously rather than only before and after correction. The test set used to trigger recalibration should be separate from the set used to report final accuracy; otherwise, the controller may adapt to particular test examples.

Calibration algorithms should also be compared at equal information budgets. A method using internal photodiodes, labelled examples, and a detailed device model should not be compared directly with a method receiving one unlabelled output intensity. The number of optical measurements, electronic operations, and adjustable controls should all be stated.

A third priority is to develop universal calibration software. Since meshes, rings, and diffractive systems all implement input-output maps, a single optimizer should be able to control them through a standard interface. The interface would expose adjustable parameters and measured outputs without revealing device physics. Generic gradient-free optimization could then treat every photonic processor as a black box. Specialized physical models may converge faster, but growing electronic processing speed will soon make convergence time unimportant.

Finally, researchers should investigate beneficial drift. Training with realistic thermal trajectories may improve generalization, reduce the need for high-resolution digital-to-analog converters, and make manufacturing tolerances less strict. The key comparison is not stable hardware versus unstable hardware at the same programmed weights. It is the best complete stable system versus the best complete adaptive system.

## 9. Conclusion

Thermal drift has often been presented as evidence that analog photonic computing cannot scale. The reviewed studies instead show that calibration can recover most task performance across several architectures. Factory characterization, online stabilization, and retraining are best understood as forms of the same computational process: adjusting controllable variables to preserve outputs. This viewpoint shifts attention from eliminating drift to managing it.

The strongest practical lesson is that calibration must be included in system measurements. Energy per event, update interval, measurement count, and pre-correction accuracy provide a more informative picture than a single phase-stability number. At the same time, the success of software correction suggests that materials research aimed at perfect thermal stability offers diminishing returns. Photonic processors need not remain physically unchanged; they need only remain learnable.

3. Kessel, A., and Orune, J. “Cloud descent for grouped control of large interferometer arrays.” *Computational Photonics Notes*, 9(1), 3–19.
4. Yaro, E., and Pell, T. “Label-guided stabilization of a photonic speech processor.” *Transactions on Hybrid Inference*, 2(4), 201–216.
5. Fennick, D. “Model-based correction in optical linear solvers.” *Review of Programmable Wave Circuits*, 7(3), 77–96.
6. Dorel, I., Mavek, S., Trinn, A., and Ulo, K. “Electronic readout adaptation under optical front-end drift.” *Machine Learning with Waves*, 5(1), 25–39.
7. Pasto, N., and Wren, B. “Three thermal control strategies for wavelength-weighted dot products.” *Resonant Computing Quarterly*, 11(2), 88–106.
8. Senn, V., and Ralka, M. “Spectral weathering for robust microring networks.” *Optical Learning Letters*, 3(4), 144–151.
9. Lenor, C., and Savi, J. “Temperature-induced displacement in a multiplane diffractive classifier.” *Free-Space Information Processing*, 6(2), 60–73.
